# August 2026

It is now 25 August 2026, and we have completed analysis of the existing
`S5b` series including the $G_6$ behavior. It appears that we have
*only* a first order transition. The transition is pegged by run
`S5b.00123` and can be seen in @fig-TvE1 below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-TvE1
#| fig-cap: Temperature vs total energy per particle. The red-dashed lines are the transition temperature (horizontal) and energy (verticle) of 0.01309 and 0.1441 respectively.

(temp <- MD2S5[ dsmean >34 & dsmean < 36, 
                .(run, dsmean, TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs)])
TEtr <- temp$TE.mean.rs[1]
ketr <- temp$ke.mean.rs[1]
dsmtr <- temp$dsmean[1]
plot( ke.mean.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data = MD2S5, xlab = 'TE', ylab = 'T')
grid()
abline( v = TEtr, col = 'red', lty = 2)
abline( h = ketr, col = 'red', lty = 2)
```

Other similar metric indicate the transition at a single temperature.
Since all of these runs were initialized, we would like to do two things
to complete series 5 (before moving on to larger systems).

1.  Add more initializations near the transition energy, as there
    appears to be a gap in energies.
2.  Perform heating and cooling as was done previously (four heating and
    four cooling).

In both of these, we will perform the $G_6$ analysis and will expand the
diffusion measurement, doubling the time over which diffusion is
measured.

## Nomenclature

The following is the nomenclature of equations:

- $T$ is generic temperature
- $E_t$ is total energy
- $E_k$ is kinetic energy
- $\rho$ is density (almost always $\rho = 1/\pi$)
- $U$ is potential energy, and $U_0$ is the potential energy of the
  system in the rest position.
- $\tau$ is the unit of time.
- $\Delta t$ is the time step (in units of $\tau$)

## Housekeeping

At the end of the last analysis
[2026-Init](Archived%20Notes/2026-Init.pdf) we added a number of data
item to the `data.table` named `MD2S5`. This contained only the `S5b`
runs, but for consistency, we need to add it into the main data record.
Recall that the full name we're using is `MD2DT.x.RDS`, where `x` is a
generation label (`C` in this instance). The following will read that
in.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DT.C.RDS
# we'll only execute this by hand.
MD2.C <- readRDS( "../MD2DT.C.RDS")
```

Now we need to merge the two data tables. `MD2S5` has 93 variables, 20
more than `MD2.C`. We copy `MD2.C` into a new memory location named
`MD2.D`, and the merge occurs in-place in `MD2.D`. After creating it, we
save it. This will not evaluate in rendering, but is here as a record of
what was done.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DT.D.RDS
#| eval: false
MD2.D <- copy( MD2.C) # deep copy
setkey( MD2.D, run)
setkey( MD2S5, run)
MD2.D[ MD2S5, (names( MD2S5)) := mget( paste0( "i.", names( MD2S5)))]
ncol( MD2.D)
saveRDS( MD2.D, "../MD2DT.D.RDS")
```

```{r}
#| label: saveMD2DT.D.RDS
#| include: false
# This is hidden in rendering, but MD2.D is read in again.
MD2.D <- readRDS( "../MD2DT.D.RDS")
```

## Plot of all Data

As we've done previously, let's plot key data items. First, we have to
melt the data.

```{r}
#| label: melt1
#  variables plotted across the row in order here.
Srn <- MD2.D[ , .( run, Series = newSeries, # Series re-name
                       #itype, 
                       Temp = ke.mean.rs, # hseries, 
                       # Values below are those plotted, hopefully in this order
                       TE = TE.mean.rs, psiavg, Cv = 1 / (1 - 256 * rtv^2),
                       Pressure = Pressure.mean.rs, psiabs = psiabs.mean.rs,
                           rtv,
                       D = Estimated / 4.0, dsmean, 
                           rseRatio = pow.rse / exf.rse,
                       LogFpD = ifelse( Estimated < 0.0, NA, 
                                   # set lower limit, drop -D
                                   log10( pmax( 1e-15, Fpvalued))))]
# First select just the columns we're interested in

id.var = c( "run", "Series", "TE") 
melt1 <- melt( Srn, id.var = id.var, #direction = 'long', 
                 variable.name = 'variable', variable.factor = TRUE,
                 value.name = 'value') 
# now each variable is its own table.
```

@fig-Transition1 shows the resultant plot. The pressure has a barely
detectable bump, but note that everything moves at the transition
energy. The data in the figure is as follows: from top to bottom, left
to right, Temperature, Pressure, Diffusion, `LogFpD` is the common
logarithm of the diffusion F-statistic probability value (the
probability that the regression occurs randomly; note that many values
are smaller than $10^{-15}$), `psiavg` is $|\langle \psi_6 \rangle|$
(the magnitude of the complex average) and `psiabs` is
$\langle |\psi_6| \rangle$ (the average of the magnitudes), `dsmean` is
the mean number of dislocations (`S5b` only), `Cv` is the specific heat
computed as $C_v = 1 / \left( 1 - N  \sigma_T^2 / T^2 \right)$, where
$N$ is the number of particles (256) and $\sigma_T^2 / T^2$ is the
relative temperature variance (`rtv`), plotted next, and finally
`rseRatio`, which is the ratio of the $G_6$ power-law and exponential
fits residual standard errors (the ratio being less than one means that
the power-law fit was better, also `S5b` only).

```{r}
#| label: fig-Transition1
#| fig-cap: Statistics around transition plotted against total energy per particle.   The vertical red dashed line is the transition energy of 0.1441. See the text for descriptions of the data.
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 6.5

xlim <- c(0.0, 0.17)
pltdata <- melt1[ TE %within% xlim,]
gps <- length( unique( pltdata$Series))
pchs <- rep_len( 0:6, length.out = gps)
cols <- rep(  c("darkred", "darkgreen", "darkblue"), each = 7, 
                  length.out = gps)
xyplot(
  value ~ TE | variable, 
  data = pltdata,
  groups = Series,      # <-- tell lattice to use Series as groups
  subscripts = TRUE,
  as.table = TRUE,
  scales = list( y = list( relation = "free")),
  xlab = "TE / particle",
  main = "Key Statistics Around Transition",
  par.settings = list( superpose.symbol = list( pch = pchs, col = cols)),
  auto.key = list( columns = 3),   # <-- legend appears
  panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups, ...) 
     {
      panel.grid( h = -1, v = -1)
      panel.superpose( x, y, subscripts = subscripts, groups = groups,
                       panel.groups = function(x, y, ...) {
                       panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)}, 
                       ...)
      panel.abline( v = TEtr, col = 'red', lty = 2)
     } # end panel = function...
)# end of xyplot( ...
```

# Adding to the Data

Below we create new data by heating and cooling, and by making new
initializations.

## Filling the transition gap.

Run `S5b.00123` appears to be in the middle of the transition, but there
is a gap below it in both temperature and energy (see @tbl-TransRuns).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-TransRuns
#| tbl-cap: Runs within $\pm0.0012\epsilon$ of transition energy of 0.1441 sorted by total energy. TE is total energy, "TEdelta" is the increment in total energy. T is the temperature, and "Tdelta" is the increment in temperature.
setkey( MD2S5, TE.mean.rs)
knitr::kable( MD2S5[ TE.mean.rs %within% (TEtr + .0012*c(-1, 1)), 
       .( Run = run, TE = TE.mean.rs, TEdelta = TE.mean.rs - shift( TE.mean.rs), 
          T = ke.mean.rs, Tdelta = ke.mean.rs - shift( ke.mean.rs))])
```

We can see that `S5b.00123` has a total energy that is 0.001 above
`S5b.00118`, and almost that much (0.0008) below `S5b.00135`. The
requested initialization temperature is the number in the run name (so
`123` is passed to `runn()`, which divides by 10,000, so the requested
temperature is 0.0123). This procedure works pretty well, although there
is some variance in the result (@fig-tinit).

```{r}
#| label: fig-tinit
#| fig-cap: Correlation of initialization temperature with final temperature. The black line is is the regression fit without an intercept. The red dashed lines are the transition temperature of 0.01309.
tinitdt <- MD2S5[, .( tinit = strtoi( substr( run, 5, 9), base = 10L) / 10000, 
                      temp = ke.mean.rs)]
plot( temp ~ tinit, data = tinitdt, main = NULL, xlab = "T Init", 
      ylab = "Final Avg. T")
grid()
tinitlm <- lm( temp ~ tinit -1, data = tinitdt )
abline( tinitlm)
abline( v = 123/10000, h = ketr, col = 'red', lty = 2)
summary( tinitlm)
```

The summary shows that the resulting temperature is about 1.08 times the
requested temperature. So the requested temperature of 0.0123 would
result in a temperature of 0.0133. Conversely, to achieve a temperature
of 0.01309, an initialization of 0.12127. Indeed, run `S5b.00121`
thermalized to 0.013008. So, we will initialize and run five more
systems all initialized as run `S5b.00121`. We will do this by
identifying the runs with an alphanumeric ".a", ".b", and so on.
Unfortunately, the `newruns()` function does not facilitate this, but
`newruns()` doesn't do much, and we can execute the `for` loop in the
*Julia* "REPL".

## Heating and Cooling

Following [HeatCool.pdf](Archived%20Notes/HeatCool.pdf)\] we set up four
heating and four cooling from series `S5b`. We ran the four coldest and
four hottest files.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-eighthc
#| tbl-cap: Temperatures, total energy, and valid status for the four coldest and hotest runs.
S5b <- MD2.D[ series == 'S5b', ] # we'll need this later
EndRuns <- S5b[ c(1:4, last(1:nrow(S5b), 4)),]
knitr::kable( EndRuns[, # 1st four, last four
                   .( run, T = ke.mean.rs, TE = TE.mean.rs, valid)])
```

We need to know the last file produced for all of these, and we can get
a hint via the following:

```{r}
 substring( S5b[ c(1:4, last(1:nrow(S5b), 4)), lrfdt.file], 61)
```

So all the runs completed with 30 files, meaning that the `...0031.jld`
file would be the last saved system state. Referring back to [2026
Update.pdf](Archived%20Notes/2026%20Update.pdf), we see that
$\beta = 0.00001 = 10^{-5}$. We showed that the approximate increase in
total energy is given by $E_t \approx E_{t,0} + 2L\beta E_{k,0}$, where
the additional subscript of $0$ indicates step zero of the
heating/cooling. @fig-diffTE shows the `S5b` energy steps.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffTE
#| fig-cap: Log plot of total energy step between samples, plotted against total energy.  The red dashed vertical line is the the transition energy, and the blue dashed horizontal line is the mean total energy step of $4.39 \times 10^{-4}$.
setkey( S5b, TE.mean.rs)
plot( y = diff(S5b$TE.mean.rs), x = last( S5b$TE.mean.rs, -1), log = 'y',
      panel.first = grid(), xlab = 'Total Energy', ylab = 'Energy Step')
abline( v = TEtr, col = 'red', lty = 2)
abline( h = mean(diff(S5b$TE.mean.rs)), col = 'blue', lty = 2)
```

So we'll use the $10^{-5}$, at the high temperature, but we'll double
that for heating at the lower temperatures. As we get into the
transition region, we'll decrease the heating $\beta$.

### Diffusion and $G_6$

So now all of of the runs are validly thermalized. The next step is to
perform diffusion and $G_6$ measurements. These measurements will add
many steps to the runs, so further heating and cooling will be done
after diffusion and $G_6$ measurements. We would like to double the
diffusion estimate time over that previously used. The previous `S5`
runs estimated diffusion over 5,000 steps (diffusion is estimated over
an execution; repeated executions provides data for averages), so we
will now use 10,000 steps. We had previously used 20 executions, so the
diffusion was an average of 20 diffusion curves.

The $G_6$ measurement is performed as an independent measurement over
`g6skips` skip cycles, and is accumulated between executions, with the
final measurement being written after the final execution. We wanted to
at least mimic @Keim2007 who averaged over 70 statistically independent
configurations. Previous work (see
[SpectralAnalysis.pdf](Archived%20Notes/SpectralAnalysis.pdf)) on
`S5b.00150` indicated that 99% of the spectral energy pf the temperature
data was contained within frequencies below $0.72/\tau$. This is a
period of `r 1 / 0.72`, so at a sample rate of 0.0177737, that equates
to `r (1 / 0.72) / 0.0177737` samples (meaning `gskips > 2`). If we
stick to the diffusion measurement of 10,000 steps with `gskips = 20`
and `skip = 50`, each execution would result in 10 $G_6$ estimates, and
20 executions would give us `r 20 * 10` $G_6$ estimates.

We need to get a list of the new heat runs. To these we want to add the
newly initialized runs with energy 121 (see @tbl-newinits). The code
below will generate the data.

```{r}
drn <- MD2.E4[ series == "S5b" & 
                  (grepl( "^.*h", run) | grepl( "[a-e]00121", run)), run] 
cat( '["', # create runs string
      paste( drn, collapse = '", "'), '"] \n', sep = "")
# Next line searches td for each run, grabs last, and extracts execution number
lfn <- strsplit( sapply( drn, \(fn) last( list.files( td,
            paste(fn, "*.jld2", sep = ".")))), "[.]")
as.integer( sapply( seq_along( lfn), \(i) lfn[[i]][3]))
```


Initially had some difficulty, as prior work left files with names like
`S5b.00010apd.csv` in the data directory, and this broke the
`createdf()` process. Cleaned these up, and the process was run single
threaded, which took some time.

At this time (2 September 2026) the procedures `g6proc()`,
`findpeaks()`, and both `trifit()` and `trifit2()` were copied from
[2026 Init.qmd](%5B2026%20Init.qmd) and into the `MD2RP` project. No
test or example files were created.

```{r}
#| label: fig-g6dataa121
#| fig-cap: $G_6$ plot fot `S5b.a00121`.
g6dataa121 <- g6proc( td, MD2.E5, "S5b.a00121", ft = 1.5, plotflag = TRUE)
```

The runs are still stored in the symbol `drn`, so we can do the
following:

```{r}
#| label: MD2.E6
g6dt <- data.table()
system.time( for( i in drn) {
   g6data <- g6proc( td, MD2.E5, i, trifitter = trifit2, ft = 1.5)
   g6dt <- rbind( g6dt, g6data$newrow)
})
setkey( MD2.E5, run)
setkey( g6dt, run)
MD2.E6 <- MD2.E5[ g6dt, (names( g6dt)) := mget( paste0( "i.", names( g6dt)))]
saveRDS( MD2.E6, "../MD2DT.E6.RDS")
```

We can see the newly added data in @tbl-newg6.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-newg6
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: A subset of the newly added $G_6$ statistics.
knitr::kable(MD2.E6[ series == "S5b" & 
                  (grepl( "^.*h", run) | grepl( "[a-e]00121", run)), 
                  .(run, dsmean, lin.rse, pow.rse, exf.rse)])
```

Next we need to process the diffusion data. Here it is done by hand,
with the functions `read_diff()` and `fitdiff()` added to `MD2RP`.

```{r}
#| label: diffproc
#| warning: false
filelist <- list.files( td, 
            "^(S5b\\.)(([a-e]\\d{5})|(\\d{5}h01))(\\.diff\\.txt)")
ddb <- data.table::rbindlist( lapply( filelist, \(fn) read_diff( td, fn)))
diffdata <- ddb[, .(d2mn = mean( D2), d2sd = sd( D2), maxD = max( Dmax)),
       by = .( Time, run)] # this creates a new DT with summaries by Time & run
diffdata[, run := gsub( '.{9}$', "", run)] # removes ".diff.txt" from run
difflist <- unique( diffdata$run) # get list of unique runs
diffproc <- data.table::rbindlist( lapply( difflist, fitdiff, diffdata))
```

So now we have the data in a data table and can look at it. The raw data
is most easily accessed via the `fitdiff()` function.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S5b10h01diff
#| fig-cap: Diffusion plot for coldest heat run.  "Ringing" with a period of about $50\tau$ is evident.
fitdiff( "S5b.00010h01", diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

The processed data as a table looks like the following:

```{r}
knitr::kable( head( diffproc[, .(run, Estimated, Fpvalued)]))
```

We can also do this in one call as follows:

```{r}
#| label: difflist
#| warning: false
rm( diffdata, diffproc, ddb) # clean up
difflist <- procdiffiles( td, 
      filepatt = "^(S5b\\.)(([a-e]\\d{5})|(\\d{5}h01))(\\.diff\\.txt)",
      MD2.E6)
```

The symbol `difflist` now has the same collection of data developed
above.

```{r}
fitdiff( "S5b.e00121", difflist$diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

The update `MD2` data table is also contained in `difflist`, and can be
saved thus:

```{r}
#| label: MD2.E7
MD2.E7 <- difflist$newMD2
saveRDS( MD2.E7, "../MD2DT.E7.RDS")
```

### Continuing Heating and Cooling

(4 September 2026) The process works, we need only continue heating and
cooling. Reviewing [S5.pdf](Archived%20Noted/S5.pdf) we can see that
things start to happen around $T = 0.00668$ while heating, and
$T = 0.0131$ while cooling. The procedure will be to perform heating and
cooling (four of each), update the table to check for validity and
resulting temperatures, make the diffusion/$G_6$ executions, and repeat.
Once runs start moving into the above temperature ranges, we'll cut
$\beta$ in half to cause small temperature and energy steps. The
transition energies are also in the range $0.13 < E_t < 0.15$. We will
continue doing this until the entire temperature range is covered from
above and below, with either "valid" runs or 2M steps.

A new *Julia* session was started, and the `BaselineSpeed.jl` file
executed so most code is compiled. Here we get the run names and
numbers.

```{r}

            paste(fn, "*.jld2", sep = ".")))), "[.]")
as.integer( sapply( seq_along( lfn), \(i) lfn[[i]][3]))
```

```{r}
   g6dt <- rbind( g6dt, g6data$newrow)
}
setkey( MD2.Ef, run)
setkey( g6dt, run)
MD2.Eg <- MD2.Ef[ g6dt, (names( g6dt)) := mget( paste0( "i.", names( g6dt)))]
cat( '["', # create runs string
      paste( drn, collapse = '", "'), '"] \n', sep = "")
# Next line searches td for each run, grabs last, and extracts execution number
lfn <- strsplit( sapply( drn, \(fn) last( list.files( td,
            paste(fn, "*.jld2", sep = ".")))), "[.]")
as.integer( sapply( seq_along( lfn), \(i) lfn[[i]][3]))
```

### Heating Parameter Check ($\beta$)

Let's try to understand what us happening here. We can look at each
series starting with its source runs. We saw above that
$E_t \approx E_{t,0} + 2 L \beta E_{k,0}$ which we can re-write as
$(E_t - E_{t,0} )/ L\beta \approx 2 E_{k,0}$.

```{r}
#| label: hcseries
#| fig-cap: Plot of $\delta E_t / (L \beta)$ (where $L = 1,000$, and $\beta = 2 \times 10^{-5}$ for the cold runs being heated and $-10^{-5}$ for the hot samples being cooled).  Each of the eight series (four heated and four cooled) is plotted in a different color.
hcseries <- MD2.Eg[ substr( run, 1, 9) %in% EndRuns$run, ] # select runs
hcseries[, ":="( hcser = substr( run, 1, 9), # og series
                 hstep = substr( run, 10, 12), # heat/cool step
                 dT = c( 0.0, diff( ke.mean.rs)), # delta temp
                 dEt = c( 0.0, diff( TE.mean.rs)))] # delta energy
hcseries$T0 <- shift( hcseries$ke.mean.rs, n = 1) # Temp at start of heat/cool
hcseries$Et0 <- shift( hcseries$TE.mean.rs, n = 1) # Energy at start of h/c
hcseries[hstep == "", ":="( dT = NA, dEt = NA)] # og runs deltas are NA
hcseries$beta <- c( rep( c( NA, 2, 2, 
                            2), 4), rep( c( NA, -1, -1, -1), 4)) * 1e-5
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dt
lmbeta <- lm( dEt / (1000 * beta) ~ T0 - 1, data = hcseries)
plot( dEt / (1000 * beta) ~ ke.mean.rs, data = hcseries, 
      col = 1:length(unique( hcseries$hcser)), xlab = "T0", 
      ylab = "dEt / L beta")
grid()
abline( lmbeta)
summary( lmbeta)
```

So the coefficient of 2.3 is pretty close to the equation value of two.
Obviously, the hot points have a large variance in the step.

```{r}
knitr::kable( hcseries[, .( run, Temp = ke.mean.rs, dT, Et = TE.mean.rs, dEt)])
```

According to the table above, the hottest cold sample (`S5b.00025h03`)
now has $E_t$ about 0.1222, or 0.008 away from our target of 0.13. At
steps of 0.00011 (which admittedly will increase as they warm) it will
take about 73 steps. The coldest sample (`S5b.00010h03`) at 0.1185 will
take 229 steps. Note that our step naming scheme (if we hold to
numerics) can only count to 99. The coldest hot sample (`S5b.00195h01`)
is at 0.158, only 0.008 from our target of 0.15, and at steps of
-0.00044, will take only 18 steps.

So, the $\beta$ for the cold steps will be doubled, and we will program
in 20 new steps. I've decided to go ahead and make 2M step runs and then
run the diffusion and $G_6$ runs. This is an easy call to `heatcool()`
followed by a call to `filerun_floop()`, but we need a programmatic was
of naming the steps. We can use the *Julia* `string()` function in base
36: `string( 37, base = 36, pad = 2)` yields "11", which will allow
1,295 steps. The sequence can be read via `parse( Int, "az", base = 36)`
which will yield 395.

On 8 September 2026, I modified the `heatcool()` *Julia* script to add a
second call to `extendrun()` if either `diffFlag` or `g6flag` were
`true`. Also added separate parameters for `steps` and `execs`, so we
can run a non-zero $\beta$, then execute a number of thermalization
steps, and then run diffusion and/or $G_6$ estimation. `heatcool()` will
also run multiple runs simultaneously via `FLoops`. The `reps` parameter
will control the number of repetitions of the heating/cooling cycles.


Processing the $G_6$ data failed on the 179'th file. This turned out to
be `S5b.00210h0i.g6.csv`, and it produced a "Missing value or an
infinity produced when evaluating the model" from `numericDeriv()`. This
led to discovering some errors in how `trifit()` and `trifit2()` handled
the coefficients. Both simply reported the coefficients they found
without `trifit()` converting them from their non-linear transform.
Nevertheless, `trifit2()` was failing on `S5b.00210h0i.g6.csv`. Since
`trifit()` does work, we can use it to retrieve the data.

```{r}

                    plotflag = TRUE, pltlog = 'xy', legpos = 'topright')
#lapply( g6210h0i$fits, summary)
fitdat( g6210h0i$fits)
```

I was not using the correct weights for the `lm()` call used to estimate
the starting guesses, so rather than get the weights right, I plugged
`trifit()` into `trifit2()`, which made sense anyway from a "dry"
perspective. Here is the new direct call to `trifit2()`:


### `xyplot` Function

We want to look at all the relevant scalars, and we will need to do this
for every iteration, so let's build a function

```{r}
#| label: plotxy

plotxy <- function( data, xlim = c(0.0, 0.17), N = 256, rvline = 0.1441,
                    main = "Key Statistics Around Transition") {
   # `data` is the data table
   # xlim are the limits of TE that will be plotted
   # N is the number of particles (needed for Cv)
   # rvline is the position of the red vertical dotted line on all graphs
   dt <- copy( data) # create a copy to shield changes.
   Srn <- dt[, .( run, Series = newSeries, # Series re-name
                    #itype,
                    TE = TE.mean.rs,  
                    # Values below are those plotted, in this order by row
                    Temp = ke.mean.rs, # hseries, 
                    psiavg, Cv = 1 / (1 - N * rtv^2),
                    Pressure = Pressure.mean.rs, psiabs = psiabs.mean.rs,
                    LogEta6 = log( pow.Estimate),
                    D = Estimated / 4.0, dsmean, 
                    rseRatio = pow.rse / exf.rse,
                    LogFpD = log10( pmax( 1e-15, Fpvalued)),
                    LogXi6 = log( exf.Estimate))
                                   # set lower limit, drop -D
                                   ]
   # First select just the columns we're interested in
   id.var = c( "run", "Series", "TE") 
   melt1 <- melt( Srn, id.var = id.var, #direction = 'long', 
                  variable.name = 'variable', variable.factor = TRUE,
                  value.name = 'value') 
   # now each variable is its own table.

   pltdata <- copy( melt1[ TE %within% xlim,])
   gps <- length( unique( pltdata$Series)) # number of series
   pchs <- rep_len( 0:6, length.out = gps)
   cols <- rep(  c('black', "darkred", "darkgreen", "darkblue"), each = 7, 
                     length.out = gps) # each should be length of pchs range
   xyplot(
     value ~ TE | variable, 
     data = pltdata,
     groups = factor(Series), # use Series as groups, and drop unused levels
     subscripts = TRUE,
     as.table = TRUE,
     scales = list( y = list( relation = "free")),
     xlab = "TE / particle",
     main = main,
     par.settings = list( superpose.symbol = list( pch = pchs, col = cols)),
     auto.key = list( columns = min(gps, 3)),   # <-- legend appears
     panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups, ...) {
        panel.grid( h = -1, v = -1)
         panel.superpose( x, y, subscripts = subscripts, groups = groups,
                          panel.groups = function(x, y, ...) {
                          panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)}, 
                          ...)
         panel.abline( v = rvline, col = 'red', lty = 2)
        } # end panel = function...
     )# end of xyplot( ...
   } # end of plotxy()
```

We want to fill out a few values for series `S5b` now that we have
heated and cooled runs. We also want to fill out `swoot`
(`specwidth / dt`, where for `S5b`, `dt = 0.0177737`), remove `rv`
(`rtv` is already there), and remove `hcser`, as it is all `NA`. Parsing
the `energy` column is tricky, and I got some help from *Duck.ai*.

That `regex` is worth an explanation. It basically matches a string with
at lest some numbers (the group "`([0-9]+)`"). These must be there for a
match. These number can be preceded by any number of characters (the
"(`[A-Za-z]*)`" group). The number can be followed by either nothing, or
either or both of the following two groups: 1) a capital letter and any
two characters (the "`([A-Z]..)?`" group) and 2) the characters "h: or
"c" and lowercase letters and numbers (the "`((h|c)([a-z0-9]{2}))?`"
group).

```{r}
#| label: regex

epatt <- "^([A-Za-z]*)([0-9]+)([A-Z]..)?((h|c)([a-z0-9]{2}))?$"
t <- c( "00325H02h1w", "00225h1w", "adf00125H02h1w", "adf0025H02", "00025",
        "abc0025", "00325H02c1w")
m <- regexec( epatt, t, perl = TRUE)
rm <- regmatches( t, m)
# next line prepends the rm list with column names, and transpose will use 
# that prepended list as column names
tb <- setDT( transpose( append( list( c( "all", "lett", "num", "suff", "hg",
                                         "horc","heat")), rm), make.names = 1))
tb
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rm( t, m, rm, tb) # clean up regex tests
```

```{r}
#| label: eparse
eparse <- function( energy, series, hcthresh) {
   # below regexec() & regatches() from Duck.ai
   m <- regexec(epatt, energy, perl = TRUE)
   parts <- setDT( transpose( append( list( c( "all", "lett", "num", "suff",
                                               "hg", "horc","heat")),
                                      regmatches( energy, m)), make.names = 1))
   # parses any leading characters, a number, and any "hnn" suffix
   letters <- parts[, lett]
   number <- as.integer(parts[, num])
   suffix <- parts[, hg]
   itype <- fifelse( number < hcthresh, "Heat", "Cool")
   itype <- fifelse( suffix == "", "Init", itype )
   newSeries <- fifelse( suffix == "", series, 
                         paste0( series, ".", parts[, num]))
   x <- data.table( newSeries = newSeries, itype = itype)
   #print(x)
   x
}
```

```{r}
#| label: Ek
MD2.Ek <- copy( MD2.Ej)
MD2.Ek[, c('rv', 'hcser') := NULL] # delete unused columns
MD2.Ek[ series == 'S5b', swoot := specwidth / 0.0177737]
MD2.Ek[, c( 'newSeries', 'itype') := eparse( energy, series, 100)]
```

From top to bottom, left to right, @fig-tranche1 shows Temperature,
Pressure, Diffusion, `LogFpD` is the common logarithm of the diffusion
F-statistic probability value (the probability that the regression
occurs randomly; note that many values are smaller than $10^{-15}$),
`psiavg` is $|\langle \psi_6 \rangle|$ (the magnitude of the complex
average) and `psiabs` is $\langle |\psi_6| \rangle$ (the average of the
magnitudes), `dsmean` is the mean number of dislocations (`S5b` only),
`Cv` is the specific heat computed as
$C_v = 1 / \left( 1 - N  \sigma_T^2 / T^2 \right)$, where $N$ is the
number of particles (256) and $\sigma_T^2 / T^2$ is the relative
temperature variance (`rtv`), plotted next, and finally `rseRatio`,
which is the ratio of the $G_6$ power-law and exponential fits residual
standard errors (the ratio being less than one means that the power-law
fit was better).

```{r}
#| label: fig-tranche1
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Key statistics (see text) for the current heating run.
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 6.5

#op <- par( mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 0.5, 0.5), tcl = -0.3,
#mgp = c(1.7, 0.4, 0))
plotxy( MD2.Ek[ grepl( "\\.*h", run) & series == "S5b",], rvline = TEtr,
        main = "Key Statistics of Heating Run")
```

### Performance of $\beta$

Remember that $(E_t - E_{t,0} )/ L\beta \approx 2 E_{k,0}$.
Unfortunately, we have a number of different $\beta$ values, and we
really need to fill these in by hand. All of the cooling steps used
$\beta = -10^{-5}$. The first three heating steps (`h01` through `h03`)
used $\beta = 2 \times 10^{-5}$. The second heating steps (`h04` through
`h0n`; 20 `reps`) used $\beta = 8 \times 10^{-5}$. We can use the fact
that the 23 negative steps are all the same to create a vector of
$\beta$s.

```{r}
#| label: hcseries2

hcseries2 <- MD2.Ek[ substr( run, 1, 9) %in% EndRuns$run, 
                     .( run, ke.mean.rs, TE.mean.rs, newSeries)] # select runs
setkey( hcseries2, run)
hcseries2[, ":="( hcser = substr( run, 1, 9), # og series
                 hstep = substr( run, 10, 12), # heat/cool step
                 dT = c( 0.0, diff( ke.mean.rs)), # delta temp
                 dEt = c( 0.0, diff( TE.mean.rs)))] # delta energy
hcseries2$T0 <- shift( hcseries2$ke.mean.rs, n = 1) # Temp at start of heat/cool
hcseries2$Et0 <- shift( hcseries2$TE.mean.rs, n = 1) # Energy at start of h/c
hcseries2[hstep == "", ":="( dT = NA, dEt = NA, T0 = NA, Et0 = NA)] # og runs deltas are NA
hcseries2$beta  <- 1e-5 * c( rep( c( NA, rep( 2, 3), rep( 8, 20)), 4), # heating
                             rep( c( NA, rep( -1, 23)), 4)) # cooling
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dt2
#| fig-cap: Plot of $\delta E_t / (L \beta)$ (where $L = 1,000$, and $\beta = 2 \times 10^{-5}$ for the cold runs being heated and $-10^{-5}$ for the hot samples being cooled).  Each of the eight series (four heated and four cooled) is plotted in a different symbol, with red beign heated and blue cooled.

lmbeta <- lm( dEt / (beta * (1000 * 2)) ~ T0 - 1, data = hcseries2)
plot( dEt / (beta * (1000 * 2)) ~ ke.mean.rs, data = hcseries2, 
      pch = as.integer(factor(hcseries2$newSeries))-1, 
      col = c( rep( "red", 4*24), rep( "blue", 4*24)), xlab = "T0", 
      ylab = "dEt / 2 beta L ")
grid()
abline( lmbeta)
summary( lmbeta)
```

The cooling series has a higher variance, with three outliers. These are
`S5b.00205h01`, `S5b.00200h0e`, and `S5b.00195h0n`. There does not
appear to be anything otherwise unusual about these runs. @fig-oddseries
demonstrates this.

```{r}
#| label: fig-oddseries
#| fig-cap: Final temerature vs. initial temperature for the three series that cause the three outliers. The three outliers are just a little below the other points. Note that while the series number was the requested initialization energy, series `S5b.00200` initialized at a higher energy than `S5b.00205`. The solid line is `T = T0`.

with( hcseries2[ newSeries %in% c("S5b.00195", "S5b.00200", "S5b.00205"), 
                 .(Temp = ke.mean.rs, T0, newSeries)], {
      plot( y = Temp, x = T0, col = as.integer( factor( newSeries)), 
            xlab = "T0", ylab = "T")})
grid()
abline( a = 0, b = 1)
legend( x = "bottomright", legend = c("195", "200", "205"), col = 1:3, pch =1)
```

### Making Tranche 2

Many of the colder samples crossed into the transition region.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trans1
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Heated and cooled runs with total energy (TE) between 0.13 and 0.15, or temperature (temp) between 0.00668 and 0.0131, ordered by increasing total energy.

setkey( MD2.Ej, TE.mean.rs)
knitr::kable( MD2.Ej[ grepl( "\\.*h\\.*", run) & series == "S5b" & 
                      ((TE.mean.rs %within% c( 0.13, 0.15)) | 
                       (ke.mean.rs %within% c( 0.00668, 0.0131))), 
                      .(run, valid, temp = ke.mean.rs, TE = TE.mean.rs)],
              format.args = list(big.mark = ',')) 
```

Only files being heated made it into the transition region, and only
three of the four series. Picking the coldest or lowest energy runs of
each series yields `S5b.00015h0k`, `S5b.00020h0i`, and `S5b.00025h0e`.
The series based on `S5b.00010` had a maximum temperature of
`r max( MD2.Ek[ grepl( "00010h", run) & series == "S5b",]$ke.mean.rs)`
and a maximum total energy of
`r max( MD2.Ek[ grepl( "00010h", run) & series == "S5b",]$TE.mean.rs)`
(in run `S5b.00010h0n`), so it is right on the edge of the transition
region.

The naming system will not directly allow us to create a new heating
series from samples in the middle of the series. We could simply discard
the heating runs that followed the three runs listed above, but that
would mean discarding three, five, and nine, respectively, or 17 20M
step runs. This is about 15 minutes of run time, and includes $G_6$ and
diffusion estimates. The key to the processing is in the *Julia*
`heatname()` function, which looks for an "`h`" character in the third
to last position. While perhaps a kludge, I will copy the three `.jld2`
files into a file with the same name, but a capital "`H`". When called
with filename of, for example, `S5b.00015H0k` this will cause
`heatcool()` to create files of the form `S5b.00015H0kh01`.

Finally, we need to compute the number of reps needed to cover the
transition region. We want to span a total energy of 0.02 (from 0.13 to
0.15) in about 40 steps (that is $0.5m\epsilon$). Remembering that
$E_t \approx E_{t,0} + 2L\beta E_{k,0}$, if the initial total energy is
$E_{t,0} = 0.13$ at an initial temperature of $E_{k,0} = 0.00668$, then
with $L = 40,000$, $0.02 = 2L\beta0.00668$ yeilds a $\beta$ of
`r 0.02/(2*40000*0.00668)`. So we'll use $\beta = \pm3.5 \times 10^{-5}$
and we'll use 45 `reps`.

That's 6 hours, 1 minute and 40 seconds for
`r prettyNum( 1000*8*45*(1 + 40*50 + 20*10), big.mark = ',')` steps, or

We should have a function that will process all the raw step data, the
diffusion, and the $G_6$ data and update the data table.

```{r}
#| label: fullproc
fullproc <- function( output, directory, dfpattern, diffpatt, skip = 1000,
         skpfrac = 1/3, df = data.frame(), trifitter = trifit2, ft = 1.5,
         clusters = parallel::detectCores() - 1, fftblock = 4096, rsblk = 500,
         maxf = 1, verbose = FALSE) {
   # output, directory, dfpattern, skip, skpfrac, df, clusters, fftblock, rsblk,
   # maxf and verbose are all MD2DFfile() parms (see).  
   # diffpatt is procdifffiles() parm.
   # trifitter and ft are g6proc() parms.
   # 
   # Suggest trying patterns before calling.
   # list.files( td, glob2rx( dfpattern))
   # list.files( td, diffpatt)
   # 
   starttime <- Sys.time() - 10 # get the time for later comparison, less 10s
   startn <- nrow( df)
   if (verbose) cat( "fullproc(): Calling MD2DFfile() with existing dt with ",
                     startn, " rows.\n")
   stp1 <- MD2DFfile( output, directory, dfpattern, skip, skpfrac, df, clusters,
                      fftblock, rsblk, maxf, verbose)
   s1n <- nrow( stp1)
   if (verbose) cat( "fullproc(): MD2DFfile() fnished adding ", s1n - startn, 
                     " rows.\n")
   difflist <- procdiffiles( td, diffpatt, stp1, verbose)
   if (verbose) cat( "fullproc(): procdffiles() processed ", 
                     nrow( difflist$diffproc), " files.\n")
   stp2 <- difflist$newMD2
   diffruns <- difflist$diffdata$run
   rm( difflist)
   # drn <- stp2[ lrfdt.time > starttime, run] # only times later than startime
   # cat("diffruns: ", diffruns)
   if( verbose) cat( "fullproc(): ", length( diffruns), " G6 possibilities.\n")
   g6dt <- data.table()
   for( i in diffruns){
      #if (verbose) cat( "fullproc(): G6 file ", i, ".\n")
      g6data <- g6proc( td, stp2, i, trifitter = trifitter, ft = ft)
      g6dt <- rbind( g6dt, g6data$newrow)
   }
   if (verbose) cat( "fullproc(): ", nrow( g6dt), " files processed.\n")
   setkey( stp2, run)
   setkey( g6dt, run)
   stp3 <- stp2[ g6dt, (names( g6dt)) := mget( paste0( "i.", names( g6dt)))]
   saveRDS( stp3, output)
   return( stp3)
}
```

This took multiple attempts and several modifications to both the
`fullproc()` code above and several routines in the `MD2RP` package. The
main problem was a memory leak caused by capturing the entire list for
files in an interior function. It appeared that memory was not being
released between invocations of the function, which eventually filled up
swap space and crashed the computer. Finding the culprit did bring some
other efficiencies to the code though.

```{r}
#| label: tranche2
#| eval: false

# heating creates files like S5b.00010h01.0031.heat.scalars.csv", so 
# pattern must be h??.????.scalars.csv
system.time( MD2.F <- fullproc( "../MD2DT.F.RDS", td,
                  "S5b.*h??.????.scalars.csv",
                  "^S5b\\..*h[0-z]{2}\\.diff\\.txt$", df = MD2.Ek,
                  verbose = TRUE))
```

As noted in the code comment above, another issue was the existence of
the `.heat.scalar.csv` files. The processing scheme is pretty clumsy,
and it was pretty evident that the diffusion and $G_6$ processing could
be parallelized to good effect, but it is hard to believe that it will
save *me* time, as I can set the processing to go and walk away, while
designing a parallel loop will take much trial and error.

We need a new `plotxy` that will create the specific heat via
numerically differentiating, and do this by the `newSeries` label.
`dydx()` is copied from [2026 Init.pdf](2026%20Init.pdf), but needed to
be modified to deal with the noise introduced by having so many
closely-spaced samples. I added a `pad` argument which will cause the
regression to span more points.

```{r}
#| label: dydx

dydx <- function( y, x, degree = 1, pad = degree + 1) {
   # find derivative over lag + 1 points
   # cat( "deg: ", degree, " pad: ", pad)
   pad = round( pad) # needs to be integer
   stopifnot( pad > 0)
   lx <- length( x)
   stopifnot( length( y) == lx)
   dlen <- degree + pad # number of points in each regression
   data <- data.table( x = x, y = y, keyby = 'x')
   xm <- movavg( x, dlen)[dlen:lx]
   dydxfit <- function( i) { # get dy/dx from points i:(i + dlen)
      c <- coef( lm( y ~ poly( x, degree, raw = TRUE), # get poly coef
                     data = data[ i:(i + dlen),]))
      dpc <- (1:degree) * tail( c, -1) # derivative of poly coeff
      dd <- polyval( rev(dpc), xm[i]) # eval poly at midpoint of data & return
      #if (is.na( dd)) browser()
      return(dd)
   }
   dd <- vapply( 1:(lx - dlen + 1), dydxfit, 1.0)
   list( dd = dd, xm = xm)
}

# test
tx <- 1:10
ty <- tx^2
dydx( ty, tx)
dydx( ty, tx, degree = 3)
(dd <- dydx( ty, tx, 2))
dd$dd - 2 * dd$xm # y = x^2, y' = 2x. these all ought to be zero
rm( tx, ty, dd) # remove these variables
```

First, let's look at the raw data, The variance of the total energy is
quite small, but the temperature fluctuates quite a bit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tvE
#| fig-cap: Total energy vs. temperature for all `S5` & `S5b` points.  Gray area shows the total range of temeratures observed, with the narrow light-blue region the small variance of the average temperature. Red dashed lines show the transition energy and temperature of 0.1441 and 0.01309
plotconfMD2( MD2.F2[ grepl( "S5", series),],  y = "ke", xlab = "Total Energy",
             ylab = "Temperature")
abline( v = TEtr, lty = 2, col = 'red')
abline( h = ketr, lty = 2, col = 'red')
```

The specific heat is the slope of the reverse graph ($E$ vs. $t$). In
@fig-Cv1 we show this full plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Cv1
#| fig-cap: Numerical derivative of energy with respect to temperature. The verticle red dashed line is the transition temperature of $T = 0.01309$. A quadratic fit with a pad of 8 (so a 10 point regression) is used as the full set of points has some temperatures very near each other.
dedt <- with( MD2.F2[  grepl( "S5", series),], {
   dydx( TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, degree = 1, pad = 1)
   })
plot( x = dedt$xm, y = dedt$dd, panel.first = grid(), #ylim = c(0,4),
      xlab="T", ylab = "Cv", main = "dE/dT, all S5 & S5b Data")
abline( v = ketr, lty = 2, col = 'red')
abline( h = 2, lty = 2, col = 'black')
```

The specific heat should be identically two in the solid, and near two
in the fluid. This can be seen if we zoom in.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Cv2
#| fig-cap: Zoom into @fig-Cv1.
plot( x = dedt$xm, y = dedt$dd, panel.first = grid(),
         ylim = c(0,4),
         xlab="T", ylab = "Cv", main = "dE/dT, all S5 & S5b Data")
abline( v = ketr, lty = 2, col = 'red')
abline( h = 2, lty = 2, col = 'black')
```
